what_its_for: Methylprednisolone is a steroid medicine that helps reduce swelling, redness, and irritation (inflammation) in your body. Doctors use it to treat many conditions including allergic reactions, asthma, arthritis, certain skin problems, lupus, multiple sclerosis flare-ups, and other conditions where your immune system is overreacting.
how_to_take: Take methylprednisolone tablets by mouth with food or milk to help prevent stomach upset. If you are using the Medrol Dosepak, follow the calendar card that comes in the package — it tells you exactly how many tablets to take each day, and the dose goes down a little each day. Do not crush or chew tablets unless your doctor tells you to. If you receive this medicine as a shot, it will be given to you by a healthcare provider in a clinic, hospital, or doctor's office.
dosing: Your dose depends on your condition, age, weight, and how your body responds. Always take exactly the dose your doctor prescribed. If you are on the Dosepak (common 6-day pack), you will start with more tablets on Day 1 and take fewer tablets each day until you finish. Never stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first — stopping too quickly can make you feel very sick. Your doctor may need to slowly lower your dose over time.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and just take your next dose at the regular time. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep them away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use tablets after the expiration date printed on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid being around people who are sick with infections like chickenpox, measles, or the flu, because this medicine can weaken your immune system and make it easier for you to get sick. Avoid getting live vaccines (such as the nasal flu spray, chickenpox vaccine, or shingles vaccine) while taking this medicine without checking with your doctor first. Limit alcohol while taking this medicine, as both alcohol and methylprednisolone can irritate your stomach. Avoid taking ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) or naproxen (Aleve) at the same time unless your doctor approves, as this increases the risk of stomach bleeding.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you experience: signs of a serious infection such as fever, chills, or a wound that won't heal; unusual weight gain or swelling in your face, hands, or feet; severe stomach pain, black or tarry stools, or vomiting blood; vision changes or eye pain; mood changes, depression, or thoughts of self-harm; muscle weakness; signs of high blood sugar such as increased thirst, increased urination, or blurred vision; or chest pain. Also call your doctor if you feel unusually tired, dizzy, or nauseous after stopping the medicine, as you may need to taper your dose more slowly.
when_it_works: Many people start to feel relief from inflammation and symptoms within a few hours to a few days of starting methylprednisolone. For short courses (like the Dosepak), you may notice improvement within 1 to 2 days. For ongoing conditions, it may take longer to see the full benefit. Talk to your doctor if you do not feel any improvement after several days.
special_populations: Older adults: You may be more likely to experience side effects such as bone loss (osteoporosis), high blood pressure, and fluid retention. Your doctor may monitor you more closely. Children: This medicine can slow growth if used for a long time. The doctor will use the lowest effective dose and monitor your child's growth regularly. Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Talk to your doctor before taking this medicine. It may be used during pregnancy if the benefit outweighs the risks, but it should be used with caution. Small amounts may pass into breast milk. People with diabetes: This medicine can raise blood sugar levels. Check your blood sugar more often and report any high readings to your doctor. People with a history of stomach ulcers, glaucoma, high blood pressure, or osteoporosis: Tell your doctor about these conditions, as methylprednisolone may make them worse.
